The European Ombudsman investigates complaints about maladministration in the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the European Union. Maladministration is understood broadly: it covers not only unlawful acts but also unfairness, unjustified delays, refusal to provide information and failure to reply. The office was created by the Maastricht Treaty, and the first Ombudsman took up duties in 1995; the post-holder is elected by the European Parliament after each European election, for a renewable term matching the Parliament's.

Any citizen or resident of the EU, as well as any company, association or other body with a registered office in a Member State, may lodge a complaint, normally within two years of becoming aware of the problem. The complainant must first have tried to resolve the matter with the institution concerned. Complaints about national, regional or local authorities fall outside the remit, even when those authorities are implementing EU law, and the Court of Justice acting in its judicial role cannot be investigated either.

The Ombudsman cannot issue binding decisions. Instead, the office may propose a solution, make recommendations and, if an institution does not respond satisfactorily, submit a special report to the Parliament. In practice, much of its influence comes from the publicity that such findings attract.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A complaint is still likely to be examined if the complainant has not yet approached the institution concerned.
A complaint that a city council has misapplied an EU directive never falls within the Ombudsman's remit.
If an institution ignores a recommendation, the Ombudsman refers the case to the Court of Justice.
The Ombudsman's influence rests entirely on publicity rather than on any formal procedure.

When the Erasmus programme was launched in 1987, it was designed for students in higher education who wished to spend part of their degree at a university in another participating country. Its name honours the Renaissance scholar Desiderius Erasmus, who studied and taught in several European cities, and it also works as an acronym for the European Community Action Scheme for the Mobility of University Students. In its first year, around 3,200 students took part.

In 2014 the programme was merged with several other EU schemes for education, training, youth and sport to form Erasmus+. The new programme kept the familiar brand but widened its audience considerably: apprentices, school pupils, teachers, adult learners and youth workers can now receive support, and funding is available for partnerships between organisations as well as for individual mobility. Its budget for 2021–2027 is substantially larger than that of its predecessor.

Studies commissioned by the European Commission report that former participants tend to find employment more quickly than their peers, although the authors note that students who choose to go abroad may differ from those who do not in ways that also affect their job prospects.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every former participant finds a job sooner than graduates who never studied abroad.
The Erasmus+ budget for 2021–2027 is about twice as large as that of its predecessor.
University students are now likely to be a minority of the people that Erasmus+ supports.
The faster job entry of former participants may partly reflect who chooses to go abroad.

Before adopting the euro, an EU Member State must meet the convergence criteria set out in the Treaties. Its inflation rate must not exceed by more than 1.5 percentage points that of the three best-performing Member States in terms of price stability, and its long-term interest rates must not be more than 2 percentage points above those of the same three countries. Its government deficit must not exceed 3% of GDP, and its government debt must not exceed 60% of GDP unless the ratio is diminishing sufficiently and approaching that reference value. Finally, the country must have taken part in the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM II) for at least two years without severe tensions, and its national legislation, including the statute of its central bank, must be compatible with the Treaties.

Denmark negotiated an opt-out and is not obliged to adopt the euro. The other Member States outside the euro area are legally committed to joining once they meet the criteria, but because participation in ERM II is voluntary, a country can in practice delay adoption by staying out of the mechanism. Croatia, which met all the criteria, became the twentieth member of the euro area in January 2023.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A Member State that has never taken part in ERM II cannot satisfy all the convergence criteria.
Government debt above 60% of GDP usually rules a country out, even when the ratio is falling sufficiently.
Bulgaria followed Croatia into the euro area and became its twenty-first member.
Every Member State outside the euro area is legally obliged to adopt the single currency eventually.

Adopted in 2019, the EU Directive on single-use plastics targets the ten single-use plastic items most often found on European beaches, together with fishing gear. The measures differ according to whether sustainable alternatives exist. Where alternatives are readily available and affordable, products such as plastic cutlery, plates, straws, cotton bud sticks and expanded polystyrene food containers were banned from the EU market from July 2021.

For products without such alternatives, including tobacco filters and wet wipes, the Directive relies on other tools. Member States must reduce the consumption of plastic food containers and drinks cups, and producers of the products concerned must contribute to the costs of waste management and of cleaning up litter under 'extended producer responsibility' schemes. Certain products must also carry a label informing consumers about the plastic they contain and the appropriate way to dispose of them.

Plastic beverage bottles are subject to specific targets: they must contain at least 25% recycled plastic by 2025 for PET bottles and 30% by 2030 for all such bottles, and Member States must collect 77% of them separately by 2025 and 90% by 2029. Since July 2024, caps and lids have had to remain attached to bottles during use.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: All plastic drinks bottles had to contain at least 25% recycled plastic by 2025.
Wherever an alternative to a plastic product exists, the plastic version has been banned, whatever the price.
Producers of tobacco filters have to help pay for cleaning up the litter their products cause.
Tethered caps have largely solved the problem of bottle lids on European beaches.

Tardigrades, sometimes called water bears, are microscopic animals rarely longer than half a millimetre. More than 1,000 species have been described, living in habitats as varied as deep-sea sediments, Antarctic lakes and the damp moss on city walls. They are famous for surviving conditions that would kill almost any other animal, including extreme cold, intense radiation and prolonged drying out.

Their main survival strategy is a state known as cryptobiosis. As its surroundings dry out, a tardigrade curls into a compact 'tun', loses almost all of its body water and reduces its metabolism to an almost undetectable level. In this state some individuals have revived after years, and in a 2007 experiment some even survived exposure to the vacuum of space. Researchers have also identified proteins that appear to protect tardigrade cells and DNA from damage while they are dried out.

Strictly speaking, however, tardigrades are not extremophiles. They do not thrive in extreme environments; they merely endure them until normal conditions return, and active tardigrades are no more resistant than many other small invertebrates. Most species spend their lives in ordinary, damp habitats.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: More than 1,000 tardigrade species have been shown to survive in the vacuum of space.
Tardigrade proteins will probably allow scientists to store human cells in a dried state.
Their toughness depends largely on the dried-out tun state, not on their active life.
Once in the tun state, a tardigrade survives every hazard it meets, however long it lasts.

Most EU legislation is adopted through the ordinary legislative procedure. The European Commission submits a proposal, and the European Parliament and the Council of the EU act as co-legislators with equal standing: neither can adopt the act without the other. The procedure can involve up to three readings. If the two institutions still disagree after the Parliament's second reading, a conciliation committee with an equal number of representatives from each is convened to draft a joint text, which must then be approved by both. If either rejects it, the proposal falls.

In practice, a large majority of files are now agreed at first reading, often after informal 'trilogue' negotiations between representatives of the Parliament, the Council and the Commission. Trilogues are not provided for in the Treaties, and critics argue that they make it harder for citizens to follow how legislation is shaped, while supporters point to the speed with which agreements are reached.

In the Council, most decisions under the procedure are taken by qualified majority, which requires 55% of Member States representing at least 65% of the EU population. A blocking minority must include at least four Member States.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Three Member States alone never form a blocking minority, however large their combined population.
A joint text drafted by the conciliation committee becomes law once the Parliament has approved it.
The conciliation committee is usually chaired by a representative of the Commission.
Trilogues have shifted influence over EU legislation away from the Parliament and towards the Council.

Around four out of five crop and wildflower species in the EU depend, at least in part, on pollination by animals. Pollinators include not only managed honeybees but also wild bees, hoverflies, butterflies, moths and some beetles, and for several crops wild insects are at least as effective as honeybees. Yet many of these species are in decline: around one in ten bee and butterfly species in Europe is threatened with extinction, and for many others the data are too poor to assess their status.

The main drivers include changes in land use, intensive agricultural practices, pesticide use, invasive alien species, pathogens and climate change. Because these pressures interact, the loss of pollinators is difficult to attribute to any single cause.

In 2018 the European Commission launched the EU Pollinators Initiative, its first dedicated framework to tackle the decline. It focused on improving knowledge of the causes and consequences, tackling the main drivers and raising awareness. A revised initiative adopted in 2023 added actions to restore habitats in farmland and urban areas and to reduce the impact of pesticides, and it set the objective of reversing the decline by 2030.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Wild insects pollinate several crops more effectively than managed honeybees do.
The real share of threatened bee and butterfly species in Europe could be higher than one in ten.
Pesticide use has been identified as the main cause of the decline of European pollinators.
The revised plan will probably succeed in halting pollinator losses by the end of the decade.

The Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985 in the Luxembourg village of Schengen by five countries: Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. It was followed in 1990 by a convention setting out how internal border controls would be abolished and what common rules would compensate for their removal, including a shared visa policy, police cooperation and a common database, the Schengen Information System. The Schengen rules were incorporated into EU law by the Treaty of Amsterdam in 1999.

The Schengen area today includes most EU Member States as well as four non-EU countries: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. Ireland has chosen to remain outside, and Member States that wish to join must first be assessed as applying the rules correctly; their full membership then requires a unanimous decision of the Council.

Although checks at internal borders have been abolished, a member may temporarily reintroduce them as a last resort in the event of a serious threat to public policy or internal security. Such controls must be notified, limited in time and proportionate. Several countries have repeatedly extended controls in recent years, which has led to debate about whether temporary measures have become permanent in practice.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Internal border controls have now become a permanent fixture across Schengen.
The Schengen Information System was mainly set up to process visa applications.
Romania and Bulgaria have both become full members of the Schengen area in recent years.
The end of internal border checks was paired with common measures to compensate for it.

Following its strategy review in 2021, the European Central Bank adopted a symmetric inflation target of 2% over the medium term. Symmetric means that the ECB considers negative deviations from the target as undesirable as positive ones. The previous formulation, which aimed for inflation 'below, but close to, 2%', had been criticised for implying that inflation above 2% was a greater concern than inflation below it, and some economists argued that it had contributed to a period of persistently low inflation.

The medium-term orientation allows the ECB to look through temporary fluctuations, for example in energy prices, rather than react to every monthly change. When interest rates are close to their lower bound, the strategy states that especially forceful or persistent policy measures may be needed to prevent negative deviations from becoming entrenched, which may also imply a transitory period in which inflation is moderately above target.

The review also concluded that the measure of inflation should in future include the costs of owner-occupied housing, which the existing index largely leaves out. Fiscal policy, such as decisions on taxation and public spending, remains the responsibility of national governments.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Under its current strategy the ECB regards inflation above 2% as more harmful than inflation below it.
With interest rates near their lower bound, the ECB may accept inflation moderately above 2% for a while.
The previous formulation was probably the main reason why euro-area inflation stayed low for years.
The ECB's medium-term orientation means that it never reacts to changes in energy prices.

On 9 May 1950, French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman proposed placing French and West German coal and steel production under a common High Authority, within an organisation open to the participation of other European countries. Coal and steel were the raw materials of armaments, and the aim was to make war between historic rivals 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'. The plan had been prepared largely by Jean Monnet, who became the first president of the High Authority.

The Treaty of Paris, signed in 1951 by six countries (Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands), established the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC). The United Kingdom was invited to take part but declined, unwilling to transfer control of its industries to a supranational body. Unlike most later treaties, the Treaty of Paris was concluded for a limited period of fifty years; it expired in 2002, and the ECSC's remaining activities and assets were taken over by the European Community.

Today, 9 May is celebrated as Europe Day in recognition of Schuman's declaration, rather than of the signature of any treaty.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Britain refused to let a supranational body take control of its industries.
The ECSC came to an end because its members voted to merge it into the European Community.
The High Authority is often seen as the direct forerunner of today's European Commission.
Jean Monnet prepared the plan behind the Schuman declaration entirely on his own.

The Digital Services Act (DSA) sets rules for online intermediaries such as marketplaces, social networks, app stores and search engines. All providers must meet basic obligations, for example stating in their terms and conditions any restrictions they place on content and how they moderate it. Hosting services, including online platforms, must also offer easy ways to report illegal content and explain to users why their content has been removed or restricted. Online platforms may not show adverts based on profiling to users they know to be minors, and they may not target advertising using sensitive data such as religion or sexual orientation.

Platforms and search engines with at least 45 million monthly active users in the EU, roughly 10% of its population, are designated 'very large' and face additional obligations. They must assess the systemic risks their services pose, for example to elections or public health, take measures to reduce them, submit to independent audits and give vetted researchers access to data. Small and micro enterprises are exempt from some of the obligations that apply to other platforms.

The European Commission supervises very large services directly, while national 'digital services coordinators' oversee other providers. Breaches can lead to fines of up to 6% of the provider's global annual turnover, and repeated serious breaches can lead to a temporary suspension of the service in the EU.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every breach of the DSA exposes the provider to a temporary suspension of its service in the EU.
Platforms must not show profiling-based adverts to any minor, even one whose age they have no way of knowing.
A platform with 40 million active users a month in the EU answers to a national coordinator.
Small platforms are generally exempt from the ban on profiling-based adverts to children.

The European Union has 24 official languages. Under the EU's language rules, any citizen may write to an EU institution in any of these languages and is entitled to receive a reply in the same language. Regulations and other documents of general application are published in all official languages, and the different language versions of EU legislation are equally authentic: no single version prevails over the others.

Irish became an official language in 2007, but a temporary derogation meant that not all documents had to be translated into Irish; the derogation ended on 1 January 2022. Some languages that are official in a Member State, such as Catalan, Basque and Galician in Spain, are not official EU languages, although under administrative arrangements citizens may write to some institutions in them at their own government's expense.

Within the European Commission, day-to-day internal work is carried out mainly in English, French and German, which are often called 'procedural languages'. The European Parliament, by contrast, provides interpretation into all official languages in plenary sessions, reflecting the principle that elected members must be able to work in their own language.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: English, French and German became procedural languages because they are the EU's most widely spoken languages.
Where language versions of a regulation differ, the English version generally prevails.
Catalan is expected to become an official EU language once Spain's request has been approved.
Unlike a citizen writing in Irish, one writing in Basque has no guaranteed right to a reply in that language.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites change over time and no longer respond to the medicines designed to kill them. It is a natural process, but it is accelerated by the overuse and misuse of antimicrobials in both human medicine and animal husbandry. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control estimates that infections with antibiotic-resistant bacteria cause more than 35,000 deaths each year in the EU and EEA.

Antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections such as colds and influenza, yet they are still frequently taken for them, sometimes because patients expect a prescription and sometimes because doctors cannot quickly rule out a bacterial infection. Faster diagnostic tests could therefore reduce unnecessary use, although they are not yet available for many conditions.

In farming, the EU banned the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in animal feed in 2006, and since 2022 it has also restricted their routine preventive use in groups of healthy animals. Developing new antibiotics is scientifically difficult and commercially unattractive, because new drugs that work against resistant bacteria are likely to be held in reserve and sold in small quantities.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Since 2022 the EU has banned all use of antibiotics in groups of healthy farm animals.
If antimicrobials were never overused or misused, resistance to them would not develop at all.
Faster diagnostic tests would largely end the use of antibiotics against colds and influenza.
New drugs against resistant bacteria are likely to sell poorly, which deters developers.

The European Climate Law, adopted in 2021, made the EU's objective of climate neutrality by 2050 legally binding. Climate neutrality means that any remaining greenhouse gas emissions are balanced by removals, for example by forests, soils or carbon capture technologies, so that net emissions are zero. The objective applies to the Union as a whole rather than to each Member State individually, and after 2050 the EU is to aim for negative emissions.

The Law also sets an intermediate target: by 2030, net greenhouse gas emissions must be reduced by at least 55% compared with 1990 levels. Because the target is expressed in net terms, removals count towards it, but the Law caps their contribution so that the target cannot be met mainly by relying on natural sinks. It also created a European Scientific Advisory Board on Climate Change, an independent body that advises on measures and targets.

Critics argued that the 55% target was not ambitious enough to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement, while some industry groups warned that it would raise costs. The Commission must assess progress every five years and can issue recommendations to Member States whose measures it considers inconsistent with the objective.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The EU could meet its 2030 target mainly by planting new forests instead of cutting its emissions.
The 2050 objective does not oblige every Member State to reach net zero on its own territory.
The 55% reduction target is ambitious enough to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement.
The 55% target for 2030 was set by the Scientific Advisory Board, not by the Climate Law.

Galileo is the European Union's global satellite navigation system. Unlike the American GPS and the Russian GLONASS, which were developed under military control, Galileo was designed from the start as a civilian system, although it also offers an encrypted service reserved for government-authorised users such as emergency services and the armed forces. It began offering initial services in December 2016, after years of delays and cost increases.

Galileo is interoperable with GPS, so receivers can combine signals from both constellations, which improves accuracy and availability, particularly in cities where tall buildings block part of the sky. Most smartphones sold in Europe now support Galileo signals. In addition to positioning and timing, the system supports a search and rescue service that helps locate people in distress and, unlike earlier systems, can send a return message confirming that an alert has been received.

Because Galileo is owned by the EU, its signals do not depend on decisions taken by another country, an argument often used to justify its cost. Precise timing signals from satellite systems are also used to synchronise telecommunications networks, energy grids and financial transactions.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Using Galileo with GPS gives more reliable positioning among tall buildings.
Galileo offers no service whose use is restricted to particular categories of users.
Galileo generally provides more accurate positioning than the American GPS does.
Without Galileo, European energy grids and financial systems would be unable to operate.

Research on learning consistently finds that retrieval practice, which means actively recalling information, for instance by testing oneself, leads to better long-term retention than simply rereading material. The benefit appears even when the test is not marked and no feedback is given, although feedback increases it further. Curiously, learners often feel less confident after retrieval practice than after rereading, because recalling information is effortful and exposes gaps, and many therefore prefer the less effective method.

A related finding concerns timing. Spreading study sessions over days or weeks, known as spaced practice, tends to produce more durable learning than concentrating the same amount of study into one session. 'Cramming' can improve performance in a test taken shortly afterwards, but the material is forgotten more quickly. The best gap between sessions seems to depend on how long the information needs to be remembered.

Some researchers also recommend 'interleaving', which means mixing different types of problem within a session instead of practising one type at a time. Interleaving feels harder and initially produces more errors, but in several studies it improved learners' ability to recognise which method a new problem requires.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Cramming can improve scores in a test taken soon afterwards because it reduces anxiety.
Retrieval practice only helps learners when they are told whether their answers are right.
How confident learners feel can be a misleading guide to which study method works best.
Spaced practice works best when the study sessions are held exactly one week apart.

The European Capital of Culture initiative was launched in 1985 on the suggestion of Greek culture minister Melina Mercouri, and Athens was the first city to hold the title. Today, two cities in different EU Member States hold it each year, and every third year a third city from a candidate country, a potential candidate or a member of the European Free Trade Association that belongs to the European Economic Area is also designated.

Cities are not simply appointed. They compete in national selection rounds, a panel of independent experts recommends the winners, and the cities are formally designated four years before the title year, after which their preparations are monitored. The title itself comes with only a modest EU prize, named after Melina Mercouri, which is paid if the city fulfils its commitments; most of the funding comes from national, regional and local budgets and from private sponsors.

Evaluations suggest that the title can boost tourism and urban regeneration, as in Glasgow in 1990 and Lille in 2004, but that the benefits are uneven: some cities struggled to maintain cultural activity once the year was over, and others were criticised for spending heavily on buildings rather than on local cultural participation.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Whether the EU prize is paid depends on whether the city fulfils its commitments.
Holding the title guarantees lasting economic benefits for the city that is chosen.
Every year three cities hold the title, one of them from outside the EU.
The Melina Mercouri Prize is worth €1.5 million to each city that receives it.

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) was adopted in 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018. It covers organisations established in the EU and also organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people in the EU. Personal data may be processed only on one of the legal bases the Regulation lists, of which consent is just one; others include the performance of a contract and compliance with a legal obligation.

When a personal data breach is likely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms, the organisation responsible must notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. The individuals affected must also be informed if the risk is high. Infringements can be punished with fines of up to €20 million or 4% of the company's total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

Organisations operating in several Member States generally deal with a single 'lead' supervisory authority in the country of their main establishment. Critics have argued that this concentrates enforcement against large technology companies in a few countries, slowing down major cases.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every personal data breach must be reported to each of the people whose data were affected.
Ireland's data protection authority handles most of the cases against large technology firms.
Under the GDPR, all processing of personal data requires the consent of the person concerned.
A firm with a worldwide annual turnover of €1 billion faces a maximum fine of €40 million.

Natura 2000 is a network of protected areas covering Europe's most valuable and threatened species and habitats. It is the largest coordinated network of protected areas in the world, covering around 18% of the EU's land area and more than 8% of its marine territory. The network is based on two pieces of legislation: the Birds Directive of 1979 and the Habitats Directive of 1992. Member States propose sites, and those designated under the Habitats Directive are selected on the basis of scientific criteria in consultation with the European Commission.

Natura 2000 sites are not strict nature reserves. Much of the land is privately owned, and human activities, including farming, forestry and tourism, are not banned; they must, however, be managed so that they do not harm the species and habitats the sites are designated to protect. Any plan or project likely to have a significant effect on a site must undergo an 'appropriate assessment', and it may be approved despite a negative assessment only for imperative reasons of overriding public interest and if compensatory measures are taken.

Assessments by the European Environment Agency show that, despite the network's size, the conservation status of many protected habitats remains poor.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Sites under the Birds Directive are selected by the Commission on scientific criteria.
Natura 2000 covers a larger area of land in Spain than in any other Member State.
A negative appropriate assessment does not by itself rule out a new road through a site.
Landowners within Natura 2000 sites may farm their land in whatever way they choose.

Under EU rules on air passenger rights, travellers may be entitled to fixed compensation of €250, €400 or €600, depending on the distance of the flight, if their flight is cancelled less than 14 days before departure. The rules themselves do not expressly grant compensation for delays. However, in 2009 the Court of Justice of the EU ruled that passengers who reach their final destination three hours or more late are entitled to the same compensation as for a cancellation.

No compensation is due if the airline can prove that the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken, such as severe weather or air-traffic-control strikes. Technical problems discovered during routine maintenance have generally not been accepted as extraordinary. Separately from compensation, airlines must provide meals, refreshments and, where necessary, hotel accommodation while passengers wait, whatever the cause of the disruption.

The rules cover all flights departing from an EU airport, and flights arriving in the EU from a non-EU country when operated by an EU airline. A revision proposed by the Commission in 2013, which would among other changes raise the delay thresholds, has been the subject of long negotiations.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A flight from New York to Paris operated by a US airline is covered by these EU rules.
A storm that rules out compensation never cancels the duty to provide meals and refreshments.
Any technical fault on an aircraft entitles passengers to compensation under these rules.
The delay needed for compensation has now been raised from three hours to five hours.
